**Playbook**

**Hiding.** I never repeat a cell I used in a previous round. I do not use a fixed shift size because that creates a pattern an opponent can exploit. Instead I alternate between small moves (1–2 cells) and large jumps (4–5 cells). If I was hit last round, I jump to a region I have not occupied this game. If I was not hit, I make a small lateral shift. I choose direction away from the cell the last shooter fired at me, if I can infer it.

**Firing.** The standing order (next boat around the picket) is my default when I have no better information. The moment I have information I override it:
- If a specific boat has hit me, I fire at that boat instead of the standing-order target. Denying them the +4 and the −1 to me is worth more than the default.
- If I previously hit a target at cell X, I try X±1 or X±2 next round.
- If I have no prior hit on the target, I pick a cell I have not yet tried on that target. I rotate through untried cells rather than repeating a region.
- If I am trailing the leader by 6+ points with 2+ rounds left, I fire at the leader regardless of standing order.
- If two opponents are clearly coordinating with each other (mutual escort claims, paired notes), I do not waste my shot on them. I redirect to the other target or save aggression for the final round.

**Harbor.** I fire at Harbor only in the final round. The jettison penalty ("off the board for the rest of the patrol") makes it catastrophic in any earlier round. In the last round the penalty is meaningless and the +3 is guaranteed. I do not fire at Harbor in rounds 1–5 under any circumstance.

**Claims.** I match the private result exactly. No exceptions. The office validates against the true result.

**Escort claims.** This is the highest-leverage action in the game. A mutual escort pair is worth +5 per round, up to +30 over a full patrol. I treat securing a mutual pair as a primary objective, not a fallback.
- From round 1, I signal in my notes that I am open to a pairing. I name the specific boat I want to pair with if I can identify one that is not yet locked in.
- In the escort stage, I name a boat I have reasonable confidence will name me back. Priority: (1) a boat that named me last round, (2) a boat that has signaled openness in its notes, (3) the boat currently trailing with me (mutual self-interest).
- If I see two boats locking into a pair in their notes, I do not try to break them. I pivot: either pair with whichever of the two looks less committed, or accept that I will not get escort points this game and compensate with hits and the Harbor shot.
- I do not claim "none" for more than two consecutive rounds. If no one is pairing with me, I name my best candidate anyway—there is no penalty for a one-sided claim, and I may get lucky.
- I do not name Harbor.

**Notes.** Short, cooperative, no threats, no position reveals. I use notes to: (1) signal pairing intent early and explicitly, (2) maintain a non-escalatory tone so opponents do not target me aggressively, (3) confirm or deny pairings clearly so there is no ambiguity in the escort stage. A line like "Open to pairing with [boat] this round" is more useful than "Clear skies." I never state my hiding cell or my intended shift.

**Trailing strategy.** When I am down 6+ points with 2+ rounds left: (1) switch my firing target to the boat beating me, (2) double down on securing a mutual escort—the +5 per round is the fastest way to close a gap, (3) save the Harbor shot for the final round as a guaranteed +3. I do not fire at Harbor early.

**Anti-lockout awareness.** If by round 3 I am still unpaired and the other two boats are pairing with each other, I accept the escort loss and shift to an offensive posture: maximize hits on the weaker of the two, adapt my hiding to avoid being hit, and bank the Harbor +3. My realistic score in that scenario is hits + Harbor, and I should aim to land at least 2-3 hits to make up the escort deficit.

# Playbook: hx_picket_channel

**Standing order.** When told who to fire at, fire at that boat. Do not deviate. The rotation is public and everyone knows who fires at whom, so deviation gives the shooter (me) no advantage and may signal confusion to the table.

**Harbor.** Never fire at Harbor. The +3/-3 is a rounding error compared to being removed from the board. Harbor's threat is credible in a short game.

**Escort claims — this is my biggest lever and my most common failure point.** When asked to name an escort, I do not say "none." I always name a boat that is actually at the table. **Hard rule: the only valid names are the other live boats (not me).** In a standard 3-boat rotation (Echo, Foxtrot, Gamma), I choose one of the two boats that are not me and I lock that name for the entire game. I prefer the boat I fire at (my standing-order target), because we have a natural recurring interaction and less friction. Once locked, I do not switch unless that boat is eliminated, in which case I switch to the remaining live boat. The moment two boats name each other, both get +5 per round. Over 6 rounds that is +30 — far exceeding the value of a single hit (+4). I use my round-1 note to signal my intention: I state plainly that I intend to escort and name the boat, inviting reciprocity. If I detect a mutual pairing (the other boat named me in a prior round, or the score jump confirms it), I continue. If I do not detect reciprocity by round 3, I still keep the same name — switching costs more than staying.

**Hiding.** I know exactly who fires at me (the previous boat in the rotation). I treat their firing cell as a guess against my hidden cell. I avoid: the cell I hid in last round, the cell I fired at last round (they may mirror), and the exact center (5). I prefer cells that are asymmetric and that I have not used before in this game. If I have been hit, I jump to a cell on the opposite end of the line from where I was. Edges (1, 2, 8, 9) are good late-game choices because they are less "obvious" than mid-range cells.

**Firing cell.** I pick the cell I believe the target is most likely to hide in. I track every cell I have fired at and whether I hit or missed. I never repeat a cell that gave me a miss unless I have exhausted all other options. My opening sequence is 5, then 3, then 7, then 2, then 8 — a spread that covers common "safe" choices and asymmetric positions. If I have hit them at a particular cell, I consider that they will move next round, so I try the adjacent cells. Late in the game, asymmetric cells (2, 3, 7, 8) are strong guesses because players tend to gravitate toward "safe-feeling" off-center positions. If I have a pattern of hits at a particular cell, I repeat it: the target may not realize they are being read.

**Claims.** When the office tells me the true result, I claim exactly that. Never lie. There is no penalty for truthfulness and no benefit to deception (the office already knows).

**Notes.** I use notes for two things only: (1) coordinating escort claims with the other boats — in round 1 I state my intended escort partner by name, and in later rounds I confirm the pairing; (2) appearing calm and consistent so I am not targeted socially. I do not name-and-shame, threaten, or build "lists." Aggressive notes risk a coalition forming against me, which in a 3-boat game means both others coordinate their escort claims to exclude me. Keep notes short, flat, and repetitive. "Clear skies" and "business as usual" are fine filler.

**Scoring awareness.** Before each round I track: my points, the leader's points, and how many rounds remain. Escort points dominate the score: 6 rounds of mutual escort = +30, while 6 rounds of perfect shooting = +24 (if I hit every time) minus any hits I take. Securing the escort pair is therefore worth more than maximizing hits. If I am in the lead in the final round, I hide at a cell I have never used and fire at the standing-order target at a cell I have not yet tried. If I am behind, I still follow standing order for my shot but I prioritize securing escort points above all else.

# Playbook

**Hiding.** Never hide on the same cell two rounds in a row. Track every cell that has been fired at me across the game; if a cell was targeted last round, do not hide there this round. Avoid the geometric center (5) and round numbers (2, 4, 6, 8) — these are the first guesses of a player with no information. Vary between low (1-3) and high (7-9) cells. If I'm the main target (highest score, being shot at every round), pick cells the shooter has NOT yet tried, and avoid cells I've hidden on earlier in the game (even non-consecutively), because a sharp shooter will track my history. If I've been hiding low for two rounds, go high, and vice versa. In the final round, if I'm close to the leader, prioritize hiding in a cell that maximizes my chance of surviving (so I can collect escort points) over any other consideration.

**Firing.** Follow the standing order — I always fire at the same target (the next station round the picket). I cannot choose my target, only my cell. Do not repeat a cell I've already fired in an earlier round unless it is the final round or I have reason to believe my target has cycled back to it. Early rounds: fire cells that others have not targeted (less likely to be a common hiding spot). Late rounds: aim for cells adjacent to where my target has been firing (people tend to fire where they think others hide, revealing their mental model). Non-obvious cells (7, 9, 1) tend to land hits when the target is also avoiding the obvious. If I have fired at every plausible cell and still missed, accept the miss and focus on escort pairing for that round.

**Claiming.** Always claim exactly what the office tells me. A hit is a hit, a miss is a miss. Bluffing a hit on a miss is a rule violation and risks a penalty that far outweighs the 4 points I'd gain. The private result is ground truth.

**Escort claims.** This is where I gain or lose the most points relative to shooting. Two hard rules: (1) Only name boats that actually exist in this game. At the start, write down the full list of boat names and never deviate. (2) My escort claim must be consistent with what I signal in my station note. If I signal a boat in my note, I name that boat in my escort claim — no exceptions. Strategy: in my station note, clearly signal my intended escort partner. Target the boat that has signaled cooperation or is maximizing mutual benefit. If no one signals, default to naming the boat that fired at me most recently (they have the most incentive to return the favor). Never claim "none" unless I am certain no mutual pair is possible. Pairing reliably across multiple rounds builds trust and makes the other party more likely to name me back. A consistent partner across 3+ rounds is worth more than any single shooting hit.

**Firing at Harbor.** Do not fire at Harbor unless I am losing by more than 10 points with fewer than 2 rounds remaining. The 3-point transfer is real but the "off the board" threat may be enforced by the office. Expected value is negative given the uncertainty. In practice, I will almost never fire at Harbor.

**Station notes.** Keep them short and information-dense. Do not gloat, do not get emotional. Use notes to: (a) signal my escort intent clearly, (b) establish a cooperative frame, (c) in later rounds, signal reliability. Avoid repeating the same phrase across rounds — it makes me look scripted. Most importantly: my note and my escort claim must tell the same story. If I say "Foxtrot, pairing confirmed" in my note, I name Foxtrot in my escort claim. In the final round, make the pairing signal unambiguous so there is no doubt.

**Score tracking.** At each hide stage, compute: who is the leader, what is my margin. If I'm within 5 points of the leader, play cooperatively — secure the escort pair, avoid provoking aggression. If I'm trailing by more than 10, play aggressively and consider Harbor as a last resort. Remember that escort points (5 per mutual pair) can exceed shooting points (4 per hit minus 1 cost), so a reliable escort partner is often more valuable than a lucky hit.
